This page demonstrates how to use the `py-qte` package to obtain quantile treatment effects in the
context of the regression-discontinuity design (RDD). The point estimator follows
[Frandsen, Frölich & Melly 2012](#ref-ffm-2012) and targets quantile treatment effect for local
compliers at the cutoff. It handles both sharp and fuzzy RDDs.

Under the standard RD assumptions, the distribution of the treated potential outcome among compliers
at the cutoff is identified through the following Wald ratio

$$
F_{Y(1)\mid C}(y)
=
\frac{
\lim_{r\downarrow c} E[1(Y \le y) D \mid R = r]
-
\lim_{r\uparrow c} E[1(Y \le y) D \mid R = r]
}{
\lim_{r\downarrow c} E[D \mid R = r]
-
\lim_{r\uparrow c} E[D \mid R = r]
},
$$

and the control counterpart is the reverse side difference of $1(Y \le y)(1-D)$. The quantile
treatment effect is then the difference between the inverses of these two complier distribution
functions.

Standard errors can be obtained via the case or the multiplier-bootstrap. The multiplier-bootstrap
allows for the computation of uniform confidence bands, i.e. confidence bands that apply to all
quantiles jointly.

The multiplier-bootstrap uniform band follows the constant-width convention of
[Chiang, Hsu & Sasaki 2019](#ref-chs-2019) and Stata's
[`rdqte`](https://ideas.repec.org/c/boc/bocode/s458789.html) package. The R package
[`QTE.RD`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=QTE.RD) of [Qu & Yoon 2025](#ref-qu-yoon-2025) also
served as a reference point.

A bandwidth must be supplied. The estimator, as of now, does not select one internally.
`outcome_grid` is either the number of weighted-quantile points used for the distribution
regressions or an explicit sequence of outcome values.

{{< include _setup-rdd.qmd >}}

```{python}
#| label: setup
from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig, BootstrapMultiplierConfig
from qte.datasets import load_ddk_2011
from qte.rdd import (
    LocalPolynomialConfig,
    RunningVariableConfig,
    estimate_rdd_distribution_effects,
    plot_rdd_design,
    plot_rdd_treatment,
)

QS = [0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90]
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=200, seed=42, n_workers=4)
UNIFORM_BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapMultiplierConfig(n_draws=1000, seed=42)
```

## The Data

The data are from [Duflo, Dupas & Kremer 2011](#ref-ddk-2011), a randomized evaluation of tracking
in Kenyan primary schools. The paper asks whether separating students into high- and low-ability
sections ("tracking") improves learning, and how peer composition and teacher incentives, both
changing with tracking, shape that answer. The authors have access to control schools without
tracking. The setting, however, lends itself also to an RDD since _within_ the tracking schools
students where assigned to a track based on a cutoff in a baseline test score. The RDD setup, thus,
can speak to a question regarding the effect of placing a marginal student into the track of better
performing students. It is the empirical example in [Qu & Yoon 2025](#ref-qu-yoon-2025)

The main variables are:

- `percentile`: the student's baseline test percentile, the running variable.
- `highstream`: assignment to the upper-ability section in a tracking school.
- `ts_std`: the standardized endline test score, the outcome.
- `tracking`: whether the school was sampled for tracking.

We keep the 2,980 tracking-school students with non-missing outcome and running variable, set the
cutoff at 50, and define treatment sharply as being at or above the median percentile. The raw
`highstream` variable is not perfectly deterministic at the cutoff, so the sharp definition keeps
the demonstration focused on assignment at the cutoff. The dataset is the one distributed with the R
package `QTE.RD`; the Stata benchmark uses the same sample and cutoff.

```{python}
#| label: lst-ddk-data
DDK = (
    load_ddk_2011()
    .filter(pl.col("tracking") == 1)
    .drop_nulls(["ts_std", "percentile"])
    .with_columns((pl.col("percentile") >= 50.0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("treatment"))
)
print(f"{DDK.height:,} students in tracking schools")
print(f"{DDK['treatment'].sum():,} at or above the median percentile")
```

## Descriptives

The figures show the outcome and the treatment probability against the running variable. Binned
means are plotted separately on either side of the cutoff, together with local-linear fits inside
the estimation window.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ddk-outcome
#| fig-cap: "Endline test scores around the cutoff, with binned means and local-linear fits on either side."
show_chart(
    plot_rdd_design(
        DDK,
        "ts_std",
        RunningVariableConfig("percentile", 50.0),
        n_bins=20,
        local_polynomial_config=LocalPolynomialConfig(bandwidth=20.0),
    )
)
```

@fig-ddk-outcome reflects the substantive finding in [Qu & Yoon 2025](#ref-qu-yoon-2025): the
outcome jump at the cutoff is small, so students just above the median do not appear to gain from
being assigned to the better section.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ddk-first-stage
#| fig-cap: "Treatment probability around the cutoff, with binned means and local-linear fits on either side."
show_chart(
    plot_rdd_treatment(
        DDK,
        "treatment",
        RunningVariableConfig("percentile", 50.0),
        n_bins=20,
        local_polynomial_config=LocalPolynomialConfig(bandwidth=20.0),
    )
)
```

@fig-ddk-first-stage shows the sharp assignment rule: treatment jumps from zero to one at the median
percentile.

## Estimation

We estimate the complier quantile treatment effects at the cutoff with a local-linear distribution
regression and a bandwidth of 20 percentile points.

```{python}
#| label: estimate
res = estimate_rdd_distribution_effects(
    DDK,
    outcome="ts_std",
    treatment="treatment",
    running_variable=RunningVariableConfig("percentile", 50.0),
    qs=QS,
    local_polynomial_config=LocalPolynomialConfig(bandwidth=20.0),
    outcome_grid=200,
    bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
)

```

@tbl-rdd-estimate and @fig-rdd-estimate show the results in tabular and graphical form.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rdd-estimate
res.tabulate()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-rdd-estimate
#| fig-cap: "Local quantile treatment effects on the Duflo tracking data."
show_chart(res.plot())
```

The first stage is one because treatment is defined sharply at the cutoff. While our results look
similar to [Qu & Yoon 2025](#ref-qu-yoon-2025) at lower quantiles (in terms of the point estimate
and the confidence band), their results do not include the _somewhat_ sharp uptick at the 0.9
quantile. Notice that they generally implement a different estimator.

## Uniform Bands

The RDD distribution estimator is the first and only design in `py-qte` that implements the
multiplier boostrap, and therefore the only one that supports _uniform confidence bands_.

A pointwise interval covers the QTE at one quantile at a time:

$$
P\left(\widehat{\mathrm{QTE}}(\tau)-z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\widehat{se}(\tau)
\le \mathrm{QTE}(\tau)\le
\widehat{\mathrm{QTE}}(\tau)+z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\widehat{se}(\tau)\right)=1-\alpha.
$$

A uniform band covers the entire quantile curve simultaneously:

$$
P\left(\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}
\left|\widehat{\mathrm{QTE}}(\tau)-\mathrm{QTE}(\tau)\right|
\le c_{1-\alpha}\right)=1-\alpha.
$$

This is the relevant object when the whole QTE process is inspected, because it accounts for the
joint variation across quantiles. The multiplier draws approximate the distribution of that process;
the critical value is taken from the supremum across quantiles and draws.

Passing a `BootstrapMultiplierConfig` switches to multiplier draws. With `degree=2` this is the
CHS-style local-quadratic fit. The pointwise SEs and the uniform critical value come from the same
draws. `band="sup-t"` uses the studentised sup-t critical value; `band="uniform"` uses the CHS/Stata
constant-width band.

```{python}
#| label: uniform
uniform_res = estimate_rdd_distribution_effects(
    DDK,
    outcome="ts_std",
    treatment="treatment",
    running_variable=RunningVariableConfig("percentile", 50.0),
    qs=QS,
    local_polynomial_config=LocalPolynomialConfig(bandwidth=20.0, degree=2),
    outcome_grid=200,
    bootstrap_config=UNIFORM_BOOTSTRAP,
)

uniform_res.uniform_sup_t_critical_value(0.95)
```
